item.base_system: High Entropy Superalloy (HESA) with nominal composition Ni47.9Al10.2Co16.9Cr7.4Fe8.9Ti5.8Mo0.9Nb1.2W0.4C0.4 (at%)
item.intervention: Solution heat-treatment at 1210 °C for 10 h, followed by primary aging at 1000 °C for 3 h and secondary aging at 800 °C for 20 h
item.processing: Vacuum-arc-melting, directional-solidification, solution heat-treatment (1210 °C/10 h), primary aging (1000 °C/3 h), secondary aging (800 °C/20 h)
item.test_conditions: Room temperature XRD, DTA heating at 10 °C/min to 1350 °C, SEM-EDS analysis
item.structure_change: Transformed from dendritic as-cast structure with carbides to γ matrix with dispersed spherical γ′ precipitates (69 vol%, 290 nm average size); γ′ solvus at 1199 °C
quotes: After the solution and aging heat-treatments, the microstructure consists of γ matrix and dispersed γ′ precipitates is shown in Fig. 2(a).
The γ′ precipitates appears to be spherical with an average size of 290 nm and 69 vol% measured by image analysis.
The γ′ solvus and solidus temperature are 1199 and 1276 °C, respectively.

item.base_system: HESA with FCC matrix and L12 γ′ precipitates
item.intervention: Heating to 982 °C for XRD analysis to determine lattice constants
item.processing: XRD scan at 982 °C with deconvolution of {200} reflection
item.structure_change: Lattice constants determined as 3.625 Å (γ) and 3.628 Å (γ′), resulting in a positive lattice misfit (δ) of 0.08%
quotes: Deconvolution of {200} reflection of XRD scan at 982 °C allows the measurement of lattice misfit at high temperature, Fig. 2(d).
Peak intensity ratio between γ and γ′ can be correlated with their relative volume fractions for determining lattice constants of γ and γ′ to be 3.625 and 3.628 Å, respectively.

item.attributed_mechanism: Co and Ti additions reduce the stacking fault energy (SFE) of a Ni matrix
quotes: Since Co and Ti additions can reduce the stacking fault energy (SFE) of a Ni matrix [22] , lower SFE of γ matrix in HESA can be expected.
By applying the γ compositions in Table 1 into the above model, the value of Δ Γ γ ( x ) are −1.0 and −0.67 for HESA and CMSX-2, respectively.

item.intervention: Tensile testing from room temperature to 950 °C
item.processing: MTS 810 testing machine, strain rate of 10⁻³ sec⁻¹
item.test_conditions: Room temperature to 950 °C, strain rate 10⁻³ sec⁻¹
item.property_change: Tensile yield strengths surpass those of reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; at 800 °C, behavior is close to CMSX-2
item.attributed_mechanism: Strengthened by low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure
quotes: The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures.
The precipitation strengthening has allowed HESA to possess higher tensile yield strengths than those of CoCrFeMnNi throughout the temperatures.
Although the strengths of HESA are lower than those of CMSX-4 and CMSX-10, its behavior above 800 °C can be close to those of CMSX-2.

item.processing: ATS Series 2330 lever arm creep tester
item.structure_change: Ductile necking (diameter 6.35 mm to 4.75 mm); rafting of γ′ precipitates parallel to stress axis (coarsened to 0.5 μm diameter, 3 μm length)
item.property_change: Creep rupture life of 114 h; creep curves dominated by tertiary creep behavior with no obvious primary creep
item.attributed_mechanism: Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure; tertiary creep behavior observed
quotes: The creep rupture life of HESA at 982 °C is about 114 h, which is similar to those of several first-generation Ni-based superalloys under similar test conditions.
The 982 °C creep curve of HESA is clearly shown in Fig. 5(b) , and there is no obvious primary creep with gradual increase in creep strain rate corresponding to an extensive tertiary creep behavior.
Therefore, the rafting of γ′ in HESA has shown to coarsen along the direction of the applied stress, which can be related to the positive lattice misfit (δ) between γ and γ′.

item.intervention: Creep testing at 750 °C and 850 °C under 159 MPa for 800 h
item.processing: ATS Series 2330 lever arm creep tester, interrupted tests
item.structure_change: γ′ size increased to 0.4 μm (750 °C) and 0.6 μm (850 °C); morphology remained spherical with no rafting
item.property_change: Creep strains accumulated to 0.04% (750 °C) and 0.25% (850 °C); no obvious primary creep regime observed
item.attributed_mechanism: Stable γ′ morphologies beneficial to resist creep deformation; dislocation shearing mechanism not applicable, thermally activated bypassing dominates
quotes: After 800 h interrupted tests, the creep strains only have accumulated to 0.04% and 0.25% at 750 °C and 850 °C, respectively.
The microstructure can be stable with high entropy γ matrix and L1 2 γ′, while the size of γ′ has increased from 0.3 μm to 0.4 and 0.6 μm after 750 and 850 °C creep tests, respectively.
Moreover, the morphology of γ′ has remained spherical, indicating that no rafting of γ′ has occurred in both conditions.

item.intervention: Analysis of creep strain rate dependence on temperature
item.processing: Plotting minimum creep strain rate versus T⁻¹
item.property_change: Creep activation energy (Q) estimated to be 290 kJ/mol (higher than CMSX-2's 230 kJ/mol)
item.attributed_mechanism: Sluggish diffusion of the higher entropy γ matrix and lower stacking fault energy contribute to higher activation energy and lower creep rates
quotes: From the linear slope of ln ε ˙ vs. T −1 curve, the creep activation energy of HESA can be estimated to be 290 kJ/mol, while that of CMSX-2 is 230 kJ/mol [37] .
Therefore, the possible sluggish diffusion of the higher entropy γ matrix and the un-rafted γ′ microstructure can contribute to lower creep rate.

item.intervention: Comparison of tensile yield strength with CMSX-2
item.processing: Analysis of yield strength data and theoretical models (strong-pair/weak-pair coupling)
item.property_change: HESA yield strength (840 MPa) is lower than CMSX-2 (960 MPa); estimated potential increase of 16% (to 960 MPa) if γ′ size optimized to 390 nm
item.attributed_mechanism: Optimized γ′ size for peak strength in HESA should be around 390 nm (vs. 290 nm actual); CMSX-2 has higher degree of misfit (-0.33%) contributing to higher strength
quotes: As the τ c is proportional to r 1/2 , the strength of HESA may increase by 16% when its γ′ size increases from 290 to 390 nm, which would contribute to the room temperature tensile yield strength increment from 840 MPa to 960 MPa.
Since the δ of CMSX-2 was reported around −0.33% [45] , its higher degree of misfit value would contribute to the higher strength.

item.intervention: Comparison of creep behavior with CMSX-2 (N-raft vs P-raft)
item.structure_change: HESA shows parallel raft (P-raft) of γ′; CMSX-2 typically shows N-raft (perpendicular to stress)
item.property_change: HESA exhibits tertiary creep dominance and higher creep rate compared to CMSX-2 at 982 °C
item.attributed_mechanism: Tertiary creep may dominate the creep response of P-rafted superalloys; P-raft lacks perpendicular γ/γ′ interfaces that hinder dislocation movements
quotes: The coarsening of γ′ in CMSX-2 has been reported to be perpendicular to the stress axis (N-raft) [37] , so the N-rafted γ′ can provide interfaces with the formation of equilibrium interfacial dislocation network to hinder dislocation movements [46] .
By contrast, the creep of HESA is dominated by parallel raft (P-raft) and without perpendicular γ/γ′ interfaces.
Tetzlaff et al . have reported that tertiary creep may dominate the creep response of P-rafted superalloys [47] , and this is exactly the creep behavior observed for HESA at 982 °C.

item.intervention: Strain-aging method applied to measure phase compositions
item.processing: Indentation after solution-heat-treatment, annealing at 900 °C for 50 h
item.structure_change: Cellular growth of γ′ occurred, resulting in coarsened γ/γ′ morphology
item.property_change: Validated measured γ and γ′ compositions via linear fitting slope of Cγ′-Cγ vs. Cm-Cγ diagram (slope 0.62, close to 69 vol% measured)
quotes: The chemical composition of γ and γ′ phase has been determined by strain-aging method [20] in this study.
Figure 3(a) shows the cellular microstructure of γ and γ′ phase after strain-aging, and the average compositions of individual γ and γ′ measured by SEM-EDS are summarized in Table 1.
The linear fitting slope in Fig. 3(b) is 0.62, which is close to the γ′ volume fractions measured experimentally, so the validity of the measured γ and γ′ compositions has been demonstrated.
